Therefore, the contract invoked by the Department of Public Works against the claim which was lodged by these three men in the Department of Labour is void, and would be so declared by the courts of my own province, and I have no doubt by the courts of any province ; because I believe it is the law in every province that every contract against public order is null and of no force or effect. Now, what X complain of is that, although for more than three months the Department of Labour was in full possession of these facts, had the accounts of these labouring men in its hands, it does not seem to have been able to take one step towards securing the rights of these labourers, but had allowed the contractors to be paid in full for their contract without exacting from them the fulfilment of that clause which the Department of Labour was specially obliged to see enforced. I say that if the Department of Labour does not see to the carrying out of this fair-wage stipulation in government contracts, what is the use of the department ? I say, moreover, that the other departments of state have no jurisdiction to decide this question, neither the Department of Public Works or any other. Under the law, as I understand it. questions of this kind are vested for decision in the Department of Labour, and it is impossible for that department to shirk Mr. MONK.
its responsibility in the premises by saying : Oh, the decision has been rendered against us In some of the other departments. It was for that purpose that I asked my hon. friend, at the beginning of this discussion, what the policy of his department was, and I understood him to say distinctly that the policy of his department was to try and see that the fair-wage conditions Were carried out ; but that if, forsooth, the labouring man and the contractor choose to stipulate a low' rate of wages, as in this case, an unfair and unjust rate of wages was stipulated, then the Department of Labour would not interfere. My hon. friend said that that was very astute reasoning. But there is no astuteness about it at all. That is what my hon. friend said, and it is that policy he has carried out in this case. I say we have just right to complain, before we vote this amount, at the way in which this matter was managed in the department of the hon. gentleman.

I was Minister of Public Works when the claim of the Racines was presented. I do not agree with the description of the powers of the Department of Labour given by the hon. member for Jacques Cartier (Mr. Monk). I would certainly not have allowed the Department of labour to manage the affairs of the Department of Public Works when I was at the head of it. I was very glad indeed often to avail myself of the ability of the officers of the Labour Department. I think they will agree with me that we worked very harmoniously indeed, and I did not hesitate cheerfully to work with the Department of Labour from the very inception of the organization. The way we proceeded was this: When a contract was to be awarded the schedule of wages was [DOT]submitted to the Department of Labour and prepared by them. The contract was signed according to that schedule, and when so signed the administration of the work remained and must remain under the Department of Public Works. When there are difficulties the Minister of Public Works tries to adjust them, and I have on several occasions been only too glad to avail myself of the services of Mr. King especially. On this occasion the Racines presented their claim. I do not remember whether it was presented directly to me by them or to the Department of Labour.
It was presented to both departments simultaneously.

Yes, I think my hon. friend interested himself on behalf of these men, if I remember right, I received a letter from him. I think they are electors of his. However, these claims were investigated with a great deal of care. The Racines are intelligent men, living. I think, in Cartier-ville, near Montreal. They made an arrangement by which they were to receive a cer-

tain amount per hour, as well as their travelling expenses and other advantages. They made a special bargain. After having investigated the case, I came to the conclusion that, as they had signed a contract, which was a fair one, they were well paid. I did not think I was justified in setting it aside. That is the position in two words. Now, the Department of Labour lias been made acquainted with the whole situation, the position has been discussed, and I think the Department of Public Works and the Department of Labour are jointly responsible for the decision that has been rendered. In other words. I rendered a decision, and no representations were made to me by the Department of Labour that my decision was wrong. That decision was communicated to the Department of Labour, and no complaint was made about it. The Department of Labour, I say again,- cannot possibly administer the affairs of the Department of Public Works. If the two departments attempted to work jointly in that direction, they could not do it. I have been long enough Minister of Public Works to be able to state that it cannot possibly be done. The Department of Labour, is a kind of advisory board, and very useful. Surely no Minister of Public Works, having respect for his position, would allow any other minister to come into his department and decide matters over his head. So long as I was there, nothing of the kind was done, and nothing of the kind was attempted. Again, I say that the officers of the Department of Labour have been very useful indeed. In the Racine case, I think both my decision and the decision of the Department of Labour-for that is what it amounted to- were fair and right.
I do not know that my hon. friend from Montreal, St. Mary's (Hon. Mr. Tarte) was here when I gave the details of this case.
I was not.
I want to tell him that I was not attacking his department.

We are discussing a pretty important question. The question is whether the Department of Labour should have the right to direct the affairs of the Department of Public Works. That is the case in two words.

Yes, that is an important point. I wanted to say to my hon. friend that in defending his department which I was careful not to attack, he has, I think, extended that defence to the hon. Minister -of Labour and I do not think the hon. Minister of Labour has as good a defence as the hon. ex-Minister of Public Works.
The ' POSTMASTER GENERAL. If I were an ex-minister it would be very good.

Perhaps. I think the hon. member for Montreal, St. Mary's, has given away the ease as to the hon. Minister of Labour, because my hon. friend says that he rendered this decision, carried it out, and paid the contractors and there was no remonstrance made whatever by the Department of Labour. That is just what I find fault with. I can understand that a minister at the head of a department which is not particularly charged with the interests of the workingmen and who really does not know all the details of the fair-wage schedule for the enforcement of which we have created a special and an expensive department-I can understand that a minister at the head of such a department might say : I find a contract between a contractor and a labouring man, tbe contract is sufficient for me, if they have agreed as to wages, I see no reason for stopping the pay of the contractor. It is here that the duty of the Department of Labour begins, because, I lay it down as a principle that this contract made by tbe contractor with these workmen is a contract which is against public order and as such it could not be invoked against them. That is the law in the province of Quebec, and I am pretty sure it must be the law in the other provinces also. Therefore, there would be no valid agreement, these men have been deprived of this $700 or $800, the contractors have heen paid in full and it is the fault of the Department of Labour. Why is it when the Department of Labour had these accounts in its possession that there was no question raised whatever as to the amount payable to these men when the Department of Labour knew perfectly well that the only way the contractors could get paid in fraudulent avoidance of this contract was to invoke this secret contract made by them with these workmen in the east ? Why did not the Department of Labour intervene and make representations to the Department of Public Works in order to secure the rights of these men ? That is the real point and what has happened in these three cases lias probably happened in tbe case of every one of the labourers employed by these contractors. I have no doubt whatever that they took all their labourers from the east. The hon. member for Yale and Cariboo (Mr. Galliher) shakes his head. Is he prepared to -say that there were only these three labourers taken from the east ?

I am prepared to deny tlie hon. gentleman's statement that in ail probability all tbe labourers were taken from the east, because, living there. I know that some of the men employed live in that town and were paid the scnedule rate of wages. You would not get men out thereto enter into a contract such as these men entered into, regardless of whether they would be doing men on the ground out of a job or not. and who are now- coming to the hon.

member for Jacques Cartier asking for assistance and sympathy. They entered into this contract knowing that this schedule of wages was the schedule of wages paid to men living out there, and knowing that the contractors could not procure men for less than those wages. Yet, of their own accord they entered into this contract regardless of whether they were doing men on the ground out of a job or not. I do not agree with the principle of importing men from one province into another to do work. I entirely disagree with it. X think it is a principle that should not be followed. If there was a way of preventing contractors from bringing men from the province of Quebec to British Columbia, I should be only too glad to see it applied.
That would be a very difficult thing to do.

I say if there was a way of doing that I would he glad to see it applied, so much opposed am I to the practice of contractors who may get contracts, taking their men from wherever they may reside and employing them on their contracts in another province. But the hon. gentleman (Mr. Monk) tries to evoke sympathy for these men
Who is talking about sympathy ? I am not talking about sympathy; I am talking about money.

Or money either. I will not argue the question of law with the hon. gentleman. I do not know what the decision would be in the province of Quebec in a case of this kind, hut, these men, if their contract is null and void as between them and Lemoine, have their recourse against Lemoine. It is not a question at all of classing them in the same way as if the contractor had gone to the city of Nelson where the building was being put up and had attempted to employ men there and to coerce them into hiring at less than the schedule rate of wages. About the agreement which these men entered into, I do not pretend to know anything, except what is specified in the contract which the hon. gentleman has read, a contract entered into by these men with their eyes open to all the facts and regardless as to whether or not they were doing any other mien out of a job.

I am very much obliged to my hon. friend, because I think he has made the case very much stronger. When the hon. gentleman says that no man in Nelson, British. Columbia, would think of working for the wages stipulated for by these men lie makes the case much stronger.
I will not allow the hon. gentleman to put words into my mouth. What I did say was that the contractor c uld not get men in Nelson to work for those wages.
That makes the case very much stronger.
For the simple reason that they would not be allowed by the union to which they belong to do so. If that is any advantage to my hon. friend he is welcome to it. That is a statement of fact.

That makes the case very much stronger, because it show's clearly on the testimony of a gentleman living out there that these men were employed at a most unfair rate of wages and therefore they a re right in claiming the rate of wages stipulated by the department of government that made the contract.
That brings up a matter that I should answer.

Perhaps the hon. gentleman would allow me to get through as 1 have not much more to say. I do not agree with my hon. friend that we should only give work to labouring men at the place where the contract is being executed. If a Canadian is a good workman it does not make any difference whether he comes from the province of Quebec or from any other province. If a contractor is executing a contract in the province of Quebec we will be glad to have workmen from the province from which my hon. friend comes. I believe the minister is a lawyer, hut he does not ansv'er my objection that this contract was null and void as against public order. The hon. gentleman says that these men entered into this agreement knowing all the facts, but that is a gratuitous assertion because I began by stating that it was only when they had reached Nelson that they found that they had a right to $4.50 or $5 per day.
There is a statement in the agreement you have read that it makes up to $5.00 a day. How do you answer that ?

I answer that by saying that these men did not know that they had a right under the contract made by Lemoine & Yiau to $4.50 a day. It was the contractor that inserted that clause but he did not tell these men. I am stipulating a low rate of wages with you but under the contract I have made with the government I am bound to pay a higher rate. It is there that the Department of Labour should have come in but failed. Everyone who is familiar with the ways of these contractors knows that when they have a chance they make an agreement of this kind with the labouring men. These contractors made a most profitable contract with the government, and they made a most profitable contract with the labouring men whom they imported from the east. Upon these three claims alone Messrs. Yiau & Lemoine pocket-

ed $800 which they wrung from these labourers.
Viau & Lemoine's tender was $25,000 lower than the lowest local tender, and so far from making money they lost money on the contract.

I will take my hon. friend's word for that, but there is no doubt whatever that when they signed that contract on the 1st of January, 1901, for $49,900, they had before them this fair-wage schedule and they must have calculated that they would pay blacksmiths $4.50 and stonecutters $5 a day. There is no doubt that if they were allowed to pay their labouring men half the fair wage rate they could have tendered at a lower price. It was the duty of the Department of Labour to see that justice was done to these men and we have a right to criticise the neglect of the Department of Labour to do this justice.

I must still disagree with my hon. friend with regard to being willing to see labourers coming from one province into another. He may he broader in his views than I am, in this respect, but so far as I am concerned, when a public building is being erected ini'a province-I will confine it to a province and not simply to a town-and when there are workmen in that province and particularly in the town where the work is going on who are willing and capable of doing the work, whether rightly or wrongly, I believe that these workmen should have the preference over workmen from another province. That is the principle I go on. I like to see the home man who spends his money in the town and who is building up that province, get work in that town when he is competent and willing to do it. Of course if there is a scarcity of labour there could be no objection to labourers coming from another province, or If a labourer comes in from another portion of the Dominion of his own motion and gets work, I have not a word to say. But I have a word to say against the labourer who contracts as these labourers did contract down here, to give their services at a lower rate than men were entitled to who lived in that province and were ready to do the work. Now, there was a consideration for these men signing such a contract. In the first place they were to be kept on during the continuance of that work and so the contractors were practically insuring them a job for the time during which the work lasted, which might be a year or a year and a half. There was the other consideration which to my mind is a minor one as compared with that, and that is that their passage should be paid each way and their board.
And a chance of viewing the scenery.
Yes, and the scenery of British Columbia is well worth being viewed by any one. Further than that, some of these men, after coming out there jumped their job.
Not these men.

I am not speaking of these men, but some men who came from the east did jump their job and that is why I presume the $50 was to be retained by the contractor until the end of the work. It was not like the case of men going out there without any consideration and accepting less than the schedule rate of wages and where they just simply cut in for the purpose of undercutting the wages. There was a substantial consideration given them and some of them no doubt went with the object of getting a trip to that province, and they could work when they went there or quit, just as they liked, and were in no way bound.
How does the hon. gentleman explain, that counting in every thing they got, they were still $200 short of the wages they would receive if they had been paid according to the schedule ?
That might be explained by the consideration of the men receiving a steady job for a year or a year and a half.
Permanent employment ?
Yes, and that is a very important consideration to men out of work.
They would not be employed after the work was done.
No, but they would have work for a year or a year and a half and they would have an opportunity of getting a little taste of the scenery and the social qualities of that beautiful province.

It seems to me that the hon. gentleman (Mr. Galliher) has missed the point, and that is, that under this Bureau of Labour employers and employees may contract themselves out of the obligation in the schedule rate.
The Minister of Labour has answered that.

Of what value is the schedule if it may be evaded by the contractor ? The case has been most admirably presented to the Minister of Labour by the toon, member for Jacques Cartier. The Department of Labour was warned before the contractors were paid off, that these men were short $200 or $300 each of the amount they would have received had the schedule of wages provided for in this contract been paid to them. Surely if a contractor signs a contract with any department of government and that contract contains a schedule of wages, the

contractor cannot afterwards employ men in violation of that schedule at a lower-rate ? No matter how steady the work to the men may be, that is not a consideration which should induce the Department of Labour to withhold enforcing the terms of the contract. The hon. member for St. Mary's issued his flat. He ignored the schedule. He said : ' These men have made an agreement with the contractor, and they are out of court so far as I am concerned.' Why did not the hon. minister take up the cudgels on behalf of the men if the schedule was to be of value to them ? If the contractor can sign himself out of any obligations which the schedule imposes, what is the value of the schedule 1

How I would have dealt with this case if I had been here and if it had been submitted to me, I will not now state, because that would be a mere theoretical statement. But I would certainly begin the consideration of such a question with the desire, and if possible, the determination to allow no departure from the terms of the contract, including the schedule price of labour. The particular case in question, as I have stated, occurred in my absence, and I had not heard of it until to-day. At the same time,
I recognize the governmental responsibility, and in that spirit must take the responsibility of all that occurred in this particular instance. What would be the proper way to deal with such a case would be a serious question for consideration. I agree with my hon. friend from Yale and Cariboo (Mr. Gallilier) that in this particular instance these workingmen were not very considerate of the interests of the workingmen of the west, when they chose to throw away the protection which the department was endeavouring to throw around workingmen everywhere, and make a secret contract which conflicted with that which the government had tried to make for them.
Does the hon. gentleman state that they were aware that they were 'entitled to receive the wage scale of the schedule ?
I began by stating that they knew nothing of the conditions of the contract with the government. They found those out when they were out there.

If they did not know about the schedule, how could they contract themselves out of it? They made a special contract. I do not know the terms of that special contract; but it is fair to assume that in making it these men knew all about the schedule.
No, no. The hon. gentleman must accept the statement of the hon. member for Jacques Cartier.
He will not ta ke the responsibility of saying
that these men knew nothing about the schedule.

They made this agreement at Hull without knowing anything about this schedule. They found it out when they reached British Columbia, and when they came to my office they asked me if it was possible that such a thing could exist.

If the hon. gentleman knows that of his own knowledge, I accept his statement ;* but I am inclined to think that he was misinformed. The contract was advertised and the schedule was public property, and the workingmen of Hull know full well the practice of the department in regard to such matters. These same contractors have had several other contracts with the government. It is well known to the working people of Canada, not only in Hull, but everywhere, that it is the policy of this government to establish a schedule of wages which is part of the contract itself.
All our works are under schedules.
If the hon. minister takes that view of the case, it is high time that the men who are working for fair-wages should be protected against conduct of that kind.

We are discussing at present the probabilities of these men having any knowledge of the schedule. I say it is most improbable that they did not know that there was a schedule. The workingmen of Canada all know what the present government has done in this respect, and they know it,
I am sure, gratefully; and these men, who chose to make this special agreement, made it. in my opinion, knowing full well what their rights would be in the absence of such an agreement. My hon. friend the exMinister of Public Works a moment ago mentioned to me that he now recalls some of the circumstances which induced these men to make this special agreement, and not to take the benefit of the schedule.
I did not understand that.

Perhaps my hon. friend will announce to the committee the statement he made to me a moment ago. If they made that special arrangement, it satisfies my mind that they knew very well whait they were doing. My hon. friend from Jacques Cartier is an hon. gentleman learned in the law, a jurist of great note in his province, a professor of law and an eminent practitioner, and he has laid down in the most unqualified language that this alleged waiver is literally void. If so, why has he neglected so long the interests of his clients and not taken out suits against these contractors to co n-

pel them to pay compensation to these men? If these men have rights, why has he not, as a zealous counsellor, taken steps to prosecute those rights ?
How does my hon. friend know that I have not done so?
Then, what is his grievance?
The law's delay.

Why has not my hon. friend made use of that great learning of his to secure to his friends their rights? I hope it will be made known to them that he has, on the floor of parliament, as their representative, as a professor of law, a lawyer, an eminent man, a man of knowledge, alleged that on all these authorities they can absolutely rely on recovery without a shadow of doubt, if the hon. member for Jacques Cartier, who knows the methods of the law, would only move his hand and put the majesty of the law in motion.

Might I ask the hon. Postmaster General if it is not his duty, if he believes that a scaile of wages should be fixed-and I understand that he has an officer for that special purpose

to protect those men who believe they should have that scale of wages ? Whait effect will it have on the labour market if the hon. minister neglects just such cases as those which have been presented to him by the hon. member for Jacques Cartier ? Admitting his contention that these men. knew that schedule and violated it, what effect will that have on the rate of wages in British Columbia and everywhere, and on those who believe in the schedules and desire to have the wages of the schedule paid to them ? How is the hon. gentleman protecting their interests ?

The hon. gentleman has a habit of asking a large number of questions and expecting an answer, and then standing his ground. If he wishes me to interrupt him to answer his questions, I will do so. It is the duty of the department to protect the workingmen in respect of their rights arising under the schedules. Not only is it our duty, but we perform that duty. I do not know what decision I would have given if this case had been referred to me; but I should have begun the consideration of the question with a judgment in favour of the schedule. But this case has been disposed of; it is out of court, so far as the government is concerned. No good purpose will be served by my expressing an opinion on this particular' case. My hon. friend the ex-Minlster of Public Works (Hon. Mr. Tarte) was supreme in his sphere. As Minister of Public Works, he was one of the contracting parties, and nothing could take away from him the right to determine the merits of claims arising under that contract. He was head of his department, and while he might consult the other ministers, it was for him to finally determine how he would wind up his contracts with the contractors. Whether I would or would not have agreed with my hon. friend, I could not say, as I am not sufficiently familiar with the facts; but I consider that it was very improper for those three men, knowing their duty towards their fellow-workingmen in Nelson-it was a very improper and unbrotherly act for them to have sought to underbid their fellow-workmen in the Nelson market in the manner they did. It may be that my late colleague felt they had no claim on his sympathy, and left them to that unerring law, which my hon. friend from Jacques Cartier says will give them a remedy, if they only choose to set it in motion. '

The hon. minister has been made aware of the conduct of the contractors, and he reiterates, in the face of the solemn assurance to the contrary of the hon. member for Jacques Cartier, that the men knew all about the schedule. He thus refuses to accept the statement of my hon. friend.

1 accept the statement of the hon. member for Jacques Cartier that these men told him they knew nothing about the schedule, but that is only hearsay evidence and is not conclusive ; and drawing an inference from the circumstances, I am inclined to believe that they knew fully what their rights were.
Notwithstanding the statement of my hon. friend from Jhcques Cartier, that these men,were not aware of the schedule and the rates of wages to which they were entitled if they worked at Nelson
How could the hon. member for Jacques Cartier know it ?	'

< Because I presume he has the testimony of these men. The hon. minister has no testimony whatever to the contrary, and yet he assumes that these labouring men were not telling the truth. But now that he has had his attention called to the methods which have been and may be adopted by men prepared to work under the schedule rates and by contractors prepared to evade the terms of the contract made by them with the government, how is he going to protect the fair-wage men in the future ?
I cannot conceive of any set of circumstances which could induce me to allow a contractor to evade his contract.
That is to allow the men to contract themselves out of the contract and the contractors to avoid its obligations.

1 did not say that I would allow the men or the contractors to avoid the contract. What I said was that I cannot conceive of any conditions which would induce me to allow a contractor to escape the payment of his schedule rate of wages.

Since the hon. gentleman's attention has been drawn so forcibly to the avoidance of the schedule rates in the Nelson contract, will he see that provision is made to prevent contractors from contracting witli men to do work for less than the schedule rates ? Surely that is a fair proposition, if be desires to enforce his fair wage schedules.

As we go on in the world we learn more. There is nothing perfect. There is no legislation which astute people will not find means to evade. If any weaknesses are found from time to time in this or the other legislation, it is our duty to remove them ; and it may not be unreasonable to devise some measure such as my hon. friend refers to. His suggestion is one worthy of consideration.

I am much obliged to the hon. minister. If these schedules are to be of any value, they must be lived up to. That is a proposition which the hon. minister will not dispute ; and if methods are being devised by contractors to make greater profit out of their men than their contracts allow, surely the matter is one that ought to be attended to without delay. Evidently the legislation providing for these schedules is not perfect, and I think my hon. friend from Jacques Cartier is entitled to the thanks of the working men of Canada for having drawn the attention of the minister so forcibly to this flagrant breach by certain contractors of their contract with the government.

I have no desire to unduly take up the defence of my hon. friend the Minister of Labour. He is well able to take care of himself. But I must repudiate the insinuation that in deciding as I did, I was in any way endeavouring to help the contractors to evade the schedule which was inserted in this contract. The case was submitted to me in a very clear way. Those three brothers were anxious to take a trip west. They, like many others, were in search of gold. The wages granted them were higher than those paid in the east, and they agreed to go for those wages. My hon. friend from Jacques Carder has been informed by them that they did not know that there was a schedule attached to the Nelson contract. My hon. friend, of course, has received his information from the three Racines ?
Is the hon. gentleman acquainted with these three brothers "
I am not, except in a literary way, because I have received a great many letters from them and in their behalf. They were all employed in the same time.
The blacksmith was employed some time after the others.

I understood that they would be employed all the time the work was being carried on, which was a great advantage. They were anxious to go, and I understood, when their case was presented to me, that they had gone out hunting for gold. I gave a decision. If that decision was not a legal one, I have no objection to its being reversed now.
Hear, hear.

I decided to the best of my knowledge. I had the written contract under my hand, the conditions were explained to me, and I thought them sufficient to justify me in giving a decision in a certain sense ; but if it is going to be the law that, under no consideration or condition, the schedule wages will be disregarded, I have no objection to having my decision changed.
Hear, hear.

All the same it is a pretty hard rule, and I am afraid we are going very far. These men are intelligent men. They must have known that there was a schedule, because the Department of Public Works has been carrying on all its work under schedules. That was well known.
Advertised.

All works have been advertised. There is not a work, I think, that has not been carried out on the schedule wages. AH the same, these men may have ignored the rule. Let my hon. friend (Mr. Galliher) make some exceptions to what he said. He expressed the belief that when a work is advertised in British Columbia, or Manitoba, or Ontario, or Quebec, only local men should be employed. That is not a sound Canadian rule.

I did not say what my hon. friend from St. Mary's, Montreal (Hon. Mr. Tarte) attributes to me. I was speaking of the circumstances under which these men were employed. When men go out to British Columbia in search of work and are employed, there can be no objection to that But when men contract at a lower rate than the regular rate to go out to British Columbia and engage in work there for the purpose of depriving other men-or at least with the effect of depriving other men-of work at fair wages. I say I do not want to see men from outside given work in the province of British Columbia under such circumstances.

The hon. gentleman (Mr. Galliher), if I understood him well, was echoing the sentiments and opinions of his province to a very large extent. I have received protests on many occasions from our British Columbia friends against the employment of men from other provinces. Such a doctrine should not be entertained in this parliament. If there are labour troubles in British Columbia, let me say, without making any personal allusion, that, in my opinion, they are due, to a very large extent to the fact that politicians are catering too much to prejudice. I do not make any personal allusions. But when even members of parliament are found supporting the doctrine, that only British Columbians should be employed on these public works that is going pretty far.

I did not say so. I made no such suggestion. Will the hon. gentleman (Hon. Mr. Tarte) rise and say that my statement was to the effect that men from other provinces than British Columbia should not be employed under any consideration ? Was it not to the effect that men should not be brought from one pro-ince into another under the conditions under which these men were brought into British Columbia ? And will the hon. gentleman say that I am wrong in that ?

I accept the statement of my hon. friend (Mr. Galliher). It is very clear. But I say I have received protests from British Columbia against the employment of eastern men, even for regular work, such as telegraphers and men of that kind. And the labour troubles of British Columbia, I say again, are due to a very large extent to prejudices entertained by people who, in my humble opinion should give other advice. British Columbia is in bad shape to-day. There are labour troubles all over. Instead of encouraging them, it seems to me we should give sound advice, and it is not sound advice to encourage prejudices. However, the Racine case is under consideration of the Department of Labour. And, if my decision has not been right, I shall not cry if it is reversed.
I feel satisfied that when the hon. gentleman from St. Mary's division referred to telegraphers he was striking at me.
No, not particularly.

The hon. gentleman says he is not striking at me particularly. I am prepared to be put on record as saying this-that where there are appointments to be filled on telegraph lines in British Columbia and there are competent men resident in British Columbia to fill those positions, I want to see those positions filled by British Columbians rather than by Ontario men. And I say that if this were the ease of a work in the province of Quebec or the province of Ontario, if vacancies were to be filled in the staff operating tel'eL graph lines, the hon. gentleman would not send to British Columbia or anywhere else for men to fill them. That is my view.

In Quebec we employ men from all parts of the country without asking whether they are English or French, without asking whether they are from Quebec or whether they are British Columbians or Ontario men.

I am not raising any question of race. But I do say, Mr. Chairman-I may be wrong, you may call it narrow if you like-that where there are positions to be filled in any province, the men who reside in the province, if they' are capable, the men who spend their money in the province and help to keep up the province, should be appointed. I say that not of British Columbia alone, but of any province.

The money spent on British Columbia works is not British Columbia money ; it is Canadian money. The principle which has been supported in British Columbia is false, it is bad ; and I take this opportunity of saying again that I have received protests from public men, from members of parliament
Yes, from me.

Not only from my hon. friend (Mr. Galliher)-he must not take everything I say to himself alone. I have received protests-it seems incredible-from members of parliament, from public men, from labour associations, asking me to dismiss men because they did not belong to British Columbia-for that reason and no other. They contended that only' British Columbia men should be employed on these Canadian works. That is a false doctrine, a bad doctrine, one that should not be encouraged. If we are going to go province by province, then city by city-Montreal against Quebec ; no Toronto men in Montreal ; no Montreal men in Toronto. Let our British Columbia friends rise a little higher ; they are capable of it.

The hon. gentleman (Hon. Mr. Tarte) should not refer to me in such a remark, because I have never asked the dismissal of a man because he is not a British Columbian. But I advocated as strongly as I knew, how the appointment of British Columbians in preference to eastern men. That is as far as I went, and I think the hon. gentleman will bear me out.
Hear, hear.

Coming back to the question of the contract, I cannot agree with the decision that the ex-Minister of Public Works (Hon. Mr. Tarte) came to in this case, because it seems to me that it Is

weakening altogether the principle adopted by this parliament. The effect of two or three decisions of that kind would be to notify contractors that the schedule was not to be taken seriously ; and when you come to that, you might as well do away with the trouble and bother-yes, and the pretense-of having any schedule at all. Now, what the hon. gentleman (Hon. Mr. Tarte), really did was this-he allowed these parties to make a contract setting aside the contract he had entered into on behalf of this government. It seems to me that is a wrong position for him to take, on the face of it. The object of the second contract was to get beyond the provision of that wage schedule. The purpose was to enable the contractor to make money
Will the hon. gentleman (Mr. Puttee) allow me a moment ? Would he be prepared to say that the schedule prices should have been paid to these men besides ail the expenses of their trip ?
No.
That is what I want to know, because that is the case after all.
No, not by any means.

I was going to mention that. I have no sympathy with men, especially intelligent men, who, understanding that there is such a thing as protection in the contract for them, will deliberately sign such a contract as these men signed* I accept the statement, as a matter of fact, of the hon. member for Jacques Cartier (Mr. Monk), but I want to say that intelligent stonemasons in this country do know of this matter. I am perfectly well aware of that ; and I have found other men who, knowing this, have gone and made arrangements with contractors for taking a lower price, believing, I imagine, that they can, through writing to members of parliament and getting their good offices, and through using the Department of Labour, get afterwards these higher prices that they have contracted themselves out of. I have no sympathy at all with such men, although I am aware that in other branches of labour men are often led to do this ignorantly, through not reading the papers before them to sign. I have no sympathy at all for a man that will deliberately go and enter into these underhand agreements with the expectation afterwards of being able to get the rate guaranteed in the schedule. But because of this difficulty, we are not going to recognize the practice of contracting out. The whole matter was before the minister at the time he made his decision, and I say that I do not agree with the decisioii he came to. It seems to me that it would have been fair to make an estimate of what these contractors should be paid in the way of railway fare and board, and deduct that from the amount of Mr. PUTTEE.
this claim, and then give these men the balance that was coming to them. But contractors should not be able to make money by making any agreement with men below the rates mentioned in the schedule. You have got to lay down the principle once for all, and as soon as it is laid down, contractors will be governed by it, knowing that these schedules are to be recognized as closely as any other specifications in the contract.

It seems to me that the question to which the Minister of Labour has attached so much importance is not an element at all to determine cases of this kind. According to what the minister said this afternoon it would have been .sufficient, in the agreement which I read, for the workingmen to state at the foot of the agreement that he entered into it knowing that it does not correspond with the fair-wage schedule. It would be possible, therefore, for labouring men to contract themselves out of the fair-wage clause without having any recourse left. From what the Minister of Labour says, the moment the contracting labourer knows of the fair-wage clause and he chooses to contract himself out of it, he has no recourse.
I never-said anything like that.

That is what it amounts to. The minister stated repeatedly this evening that if these three men knew there was a fair-wage clause and they chose to make this contract, he thought the decision rendered could not be appealed from.
I never uttered anything open to such an interpretation.

Then the Minister of Labour-does not think that the knowledge by the labourer who contracts himself out of the fair-wage clause is an objection to his obtaining recourse, and that is my opinion. That is the opinion at present of the Minister of Labour. It is easy to conceive circumstances where a labouring man, being in want of work, although he knows the existence of the fair-wage clause, will make a contract with a contractor willing to give him steady work say for two months for $1 a day, when he knows that under a clause of the government contract he would be entitled to $2. Even under those circumstances, that man has a recourse, and it is for the government to see that he is paid the full amount of his wages, although he contracted to serve for $1 a day. Otherwise it is no use trying to carry out these clauses at all, they are nothing but a delusion. Now, in regard to these three men, I wish to say this, that I do not think the hon. member for St. Mary's, Montreal, knows them. They are all skilled workmen, though they are uneducated. I have a letter from one of

them written in French, which I would be willing to hand to my hon. friend, and he will see that the writer is an illiterate man. They heard when they reached Nelson that they had a right to higher wages. They carried out their contract, and on their return to Montreal they came to my office, as they live in my constituency, and asked me to write the Department of Labour to find out if they were not entitled to higher pay under the fair-wage schedule. These were not the words they used, but they understood there was a stipulation in the contract made by the government with Yiau & Le-moine by which they were entitled to higher wages. The minister will find in my correspondence that I did make that inquiry, and when we got the facts from the Department of Labour we made our claim. They never knew of this fair-wage clause, and I do not think there are many labouring men, even stonecutters or blacksmiths, who know anything about the fair-wage clause.

I have a higher opinion of the intelligence of stone-tnasons and mechanics than my hon. friend. The fact that the government inserts a fair-wage schedule in contracts I think is generally known by the mechanics of Canada. The policy has been in force for some time, it was begun some years ago, and has been gradually adopted by one department after another until now it is the policy of all departments. Of course, it is easy to be wise after the fact, but I ithink that in dealing with a case of this kind one should avoid giving inducements to violate the spirit of this agreement. A workingman who knows that the government has taken the trouble to try to secure him a fair wage, and who deliberately disregards that arrangement and adopts another course calculated to injure his fellow-workingman, takes a course that I think does not appeal to one's sympathy. They do an unbrotherly act in invading the labour market of others and trying to under-bid their fellow-workingmen. If they choose to go to that other market and sell their labour at the market price, that is another thing. After this question was brought to my attention to-day I began to consider how it should be dealt with, and I will mention one method that occurred to me. I think there should be no possibility of a contractor gaining by disregarding the schedule. I am not aware whether contractors, as a rule, or at all, attempt to evade the terms of the contract.

Would my hon. friend allow me ? I remember very well that the contractors stated to me that they had not disregarded the schedule of wages, because there were advantages attached to the arrangement which were an equivalent for the deduction in the rate of wages. I remember that was one of the considerations that induced me to make these people stand by
their agreement. Let my hon. friend from Jacques Cartier inform himself about these men. Let me tell him that these French Canadian artisans are just as bright as those of any other race. They know all about the schedule of wages.
What were the special advantages they were getting under this arrangement that they would not have had under the schedule ?
The special advantages were that their travelling expenses were paid.
That was taken out of their wages.

I know ; but they had not money to go up there. They were anxious to go. Of course, I state what was reported to me. They were anxious to go, and that is the reason why they made a special agreement. There were three of them. It cost a certain amount of money to go out there. The contractor agreed to pay their trip. It was a large amount of money. I do not remember whether the return trip was paid or not.
Yes, it was paid out of their wages. How does my hon. friend know that they desired to go out there ? The contractors stated that ?
Yes, it was stated to me.
Did the hon. gentleman hear the men as well as the contractor before he came to a decision ?

Yes, the case was stated to me by my friend from the Department of Labour, and I think I got a letter from the hon. member for Jacques Cartier too. I gave a great deal of attention to the case. Of course, I do not know whether I have been wrong in the interpretation of the law, or whether the contractors had any right whatever to depart from the schedule. Perhaps I have been wrong.

I was going to say that in a matter of this kind there should be no inducement to either party to depart from the schedule. As to a private stipulation for contracting out. the rule adopted may not be sufficient. I think that precautions should be taken to prevent a contractor gaining from such a stipulation. The pressure will always come from the contractor. He will get a contract, which on its face requires him to pay a certain rate of wages. He will make his calculations accordingly and if he is successful in getting the men to work at a lower wage he thereby makes an undue profit. It may not be unreasonable to have a clause in the contract that if it is disclosed that in any case the contractor did not pay the schedule rate of wages he should lose that amount and by that amount his contract price should he reduced. I do not say that

that would be a proper remedy in all cases, but it would have the result that when the settlement was made he should not be permitted to gain by inducing the workmen to contract out of the schedule. My deputy informs me that in a large number of cases applications have been made to the department on behalf of the workmen and that in some sixty odd cases, in fact in every case except the present one, the department was instrumental in securing to the workmen the schedule rate of wages. This is the only case where the schedule was not enforced literally and it may be, that, as the ex-Minister of Public Works (Hon. Mr. Tarte) says, the men obtained the equivalent of the schedule rate. At all events, that was the suggestion of my hon. friend in dealing with the case, so that it appears after all that he was, in his judgment, endeavouring to live up to the spirit of the agreement by seeing that they got what he deemed to be substantially the schedule rate. Of course, if a large sum of money was advanced to these men to take them across the continent and they did not work it out I do not know what remedy the contractors would have. These are doubtless very honourable men who would not have broken their contract, but there are instances in which travelling expenses have been paid in advance and have not been worked out and in that case the contractor would be the loser. The contractors in this instance have run the risk. Whether they did run a real risk I do not know. I assume the contrary because we are told by the hon. member for Jacques Cartier that when they reached Kaslo they learned what the schedule rates were and they, notwithstanding, proceeded to work. It might be supposed that if their employers were with them at the time when they learned what their rights were they would have made a demand upon their employers.
They would have been fired probably if they had done so.
That may be an explanation for not doing it, but Ordinarily when a person discovers that a wrong has been done him he is ussually found asserting his claim at an early day.
Would the hon. member for .Jacques Cartier tell me how long these men have been employed out there ?

I would like to say that if these questions are to be decided not by the Department of Labour but by the department interested in the contract it would possibly be better before coming to a decision to hear both parties. They began work-this is one of the accounts-on the 4th September, 1901. They worked through September, October, December, January, 1902. February, March, April and May.
They complained only when they came back here ?

I stated that they became aware when they were out there, probably by contact with other workmen, that they were getting less than the others. They came to my office and asked me to find out what were their rights. I wrote to the department to find out their rights as I did not know myself any more than they did. Then I got the schedule and found, out the conditions and they made their claim.

There will be no hope of stopping this kind of business unless the hon. minister penalizes the contractor every time he does anything of this kind. According to the statement of my hon. friend from Jacques Cartier these men were not compensated to the extent of $200 or $300 each, which compensation was due them if they had been paid the scheduled rate of wages. I would suggest to the hon. minister that if this matter is not finally closed he should take steps to collect that sum for these men.
I think there is a sum of money due the contractors yet.
If the hon. minister wishes to give evidence of a bona fide desire to establish a fair rate of wages he will see that an effort is made to secure to these men the money that is due them.

If the hon. gentleman suggests that I am not giving a bona fide desire to establish a fair rate of wages simply because of that isolated transaction occurring, the hon. gentleman does not to my mind make a fair suggestion.

Now that the hon. gentleman has had his attention drawn to the matter I am sure we will only need to remind him of the fact, that, as the hon. ex-Minister of Public Works says, there is some money due to these contractors, to secure his intervention on behalf of these men. It is a serious matter, and I think a violation of a contract made between the contractor and the Department of Public Works should be visited with some penalty. It would be a deterrent to some other contractors from doing the same thing and it would save the hon. gentleman's department possibly from a great deal of criticism. The hon. gentleman made the statement in the earlier part of the evening that hon. gentlemen on this side of the House had objected to the remuneration paid to persons who act as correspondents of the ' Labour Gazette.' I would ask the hon. gentleman when that complaint was made and who made it ?
I understand that in the session of 1901 some hon. gentleman opposite took the attitude.
The minister made a very much stronger statement earlier in the evening.
I said exactly then what I said now.

The minister then said that members on this side of the House objected to the amounts paid to these correspondents as being too large, and that since we had changed our minds and were advocating higher wages now.
I said that I understood hon. gentlemen on the other side some time ago took exception to the salaries of the correspondents as being too high, and that now they took exception to them being too low.
The minister will be able to say who made such statements ?
I was not present at the time, but, that is what I understood.
The hon. gentleman does not know of his own knowledge ?
I never said anything different from what I say now.

The minister stated that these correspondents sent in a lot of tabulated statements with schedules of statistics. \Vhat becomes of them when they are sent to the department ? Are the reports made up from the statistics, or do the correspondents send the letter press as we have it published ?
They fill up the schedules with such observations as they seie lit to make, and their observations are edited by the department for the purposes of the ' Gazetted
The editor of an ordinary newspaper has very great latitude and he publishes what he thinks desirable. Do those who edit the ' Gazette ' change in any particular the reports sent in ?
The exact language Is not used because it may not be proper for publication, but the substance of the reports is adhered to strictly and the originals are on file.
I see Mr. Phillips Thompson makes a very elaborate report for July, Is this printed just as he sent it in ?
Mr. Thompson is an exceptionally good correspondent-
I am not disputing that.
And his reports are so well worded that it is rarely that there are any variations from the originals.
Is the July report printed just as Mr. Thompson sent it in ?
I am not able to answer categorically the question, but the hon. gentleman may rely upon it that it is substantially his report.
How often are these fair wage schedules made up ? The minister knows that the conditions are continuously changing and the cost of living is increasing rapidly throughout Canada.
On the occasion of each schedule being prepared, the department informs those, and fills up that schedule from information up to that time.
Is that the duty of the fair-wage officer ?
Yes.
How does he obtain the information ?
As a rule he visits the locality where the work is going to be performed.

I want to draw the attention of the minister and his deputy who is present, to statements that have been made during the past two or three days by a number of our fellow subjects who have come out from the old country. I refer to certain Scotch moulders who have been induced to come out here as they allege under false pretenses. It is a very serious state of things, and one that should be put an end to at the earliest possible moment. The ' Montreal Star ' of yesterday, the ' Toronto News ' of yesterday, and the Toronto papers of to-day contain statements respecting the treatment which these men have received. There is also a statement from the Canada Foundry Company as to the way they have been treated. It is a serious matter, if, as alleged, lpO or 170 moulders were induced to come out to this country under false pretenses and are now making arrangements in Montreal for the purpose of securing then-passage back to the old country. Should these Scotch moulders go back in the state of mind that they apparently are now in, it will certainly give this country a black eye, and we ought to have some report from the minister or his deputy as to what steps have been taken to inquire into the grievances Which these moulders claim they labour under. I read in yesterday's Toronto * News ' a telegram from Montreal as follows :
Montreal, Que., July 21.-A committee of ten, representing the Scotch iron moulders who were brought to this country to work for the Canada Foundry Company, at Toronto, is in the city making arrangements to have the whole party of 170 men taken hack to the old country.
They claim they were brought to Canada under misrepresentations. It was represented to them that a colony was being founded at Toronto, and big works established, and they had no idea a strike was on. there. They say

they practically had to fight their way out of the works.
On the steamer coming out they were told that a strike was on. and, after stormy meetings. decided to go to Toronto and see how the original representations compared with circumstances,
The Montreal 'Star' of yesterday under a large type heading ' Indignant Scotch Moulders ' ' to sue government officials for $50,000.' Says :
There is considerable excitement among the iron trades men of this city to-day, as a result of several of the iron moulders that were brought from Scotland to work in the Canada Iron Foundry, at Toronto Junction, where there is a strike on, arriving in the city.	.
The mem were taken to 132 St. James street, the headquarters of the Iron Moulders' Union. Among oihers were Messrs. Thomas Robertson, of 90 King street, Govan, Scotland, a native of Saltcoats, Ayrshire, and John Thompson, 115 Brighton street, Govan, Scotland.
When seen by a ' Star ' reporter, Mr. Thompson made the following statement :-
'We have had some desperate fighting since we left Glasgow, and to say that we have been grossly deceived is putting it mildly. We were engaged by Mr. William Laurie, of 322 St. Vincent street. Glasgow, Scotland, to work in the Canada Iron Foundry, at Toronto Junction. This man made a declaration to us that there wras no strike on in Canada. He said that h** wias co-operating with the Canadian government immigration agents in securing skilled mechanics for the Dominion of Canada where there was a great scarcity of labour of all kinds.
Large posters were put up all over the town advertising for 22,000 skilled mechanics to go to Toronto, Canada, where there were great extensions of work in progress, and where a new colony was being founded. All kinds of inducements were held out to us. We were to be given a home free, and our wages was to be $16.50 per Aveek, of fifty-five hours, and we were guaranteed two years' work, and they promised to bring out our wives and children.
When we 'were a few days on the ocean Ave were informed by a man named Graeme Hunter, that he was also co-operating with the government agents in securing skilled mechanics for Canada ; that there was a strike on at Toronto, and that we would be expected to put up a great fight against the strikers if necessary. We did not know Avhait to do. but resolved to go on to Toronto after we reached Quebec. There were 170 of us in the party, and we made it interesting for Hunter and the other agents all the way from Quebec to Toronto. Th'e train did not stop at the Toronto station.. We were run -into the Avorks by a side track, like cattle, where there were tents erected for our accommodation.
We were then informed of the true situation. We absolutely refused to go to work, whereupon the officials refused to give us our baggage. They tried to make us go to work by threatening us with being throA\rn into prison for having disregarded an agreement. Th*v used the police, but we fought our way out of the Avorks and we marched to the Toronto Iron Moulders Hull. Some of our party were pretty roughly handled, but none of the men were seriously injured, except Robertson. Avho w'as nearly chocked to death.
We were praoticailly prisoners from Quebec to Toronto, and we were almost, hounded to death.

We were no! allowed to talk to any person. The agreement was that the company was to keep $37 out of our wages for our passage. We cannot condemn the immigration policy of the Dominion government too strongly. All kinds of deceiving advertisements are distributed throughout Scotland, and there is now, no doubt, but the old country people are being led astray. Many of them are being brought to this country under false pretenses. We intend to take an action against the government officials as Avelil as the company tor $50,000 damages. We have our written contract specifically stating that there Avas no strike on in the iron foundries at Toronto.
There will be a mass meeting of the Iron Moulders Union to-morrow evening at 132 St. James abreet, when the whole situation will be discussed. The Scotchmen will be at the meeting and they Avill produce the agreement and all papers in connection with their trip to Toronto.
The Scotchmen are bright, intelligent workmen. They are thickset and appear to be very poAverful.
It seems to me, in view of the conflicting statements^ made, the one by the Canada Foundry Company, and the other by these men, that it is the duty of the Department of Labour, if it has not done so, to begin an examination of the conditions and of the statements made by both parties. It would be a matter to tie regretted if men should be induced to come to this country under false pretenses, especially as it appears that these men are going to return home. I would ask the hon. minister if he has sent his deputy, or his fair-wage officer, or any other officer, to Toronto or Montreal to ascertain whether these statements are well founded ?

I would draw the attention of the hon. minister to this fact, that these men evidently feel that they have been deceived, and that they are labouring under a grievance. The fact that they have elected to go to the premier of Ontario surely is not sufficient to warrant the hon. gentleman in withholding his hand ? I do not for a moment affirm that the statement made by either of these parties is correct. But it is a matter of vital importance, 1 submit most respectfully, that the officers of the department should ascertain from these men, who are about to leave Canada and go back to Scotland, their side of the case ; and then it would be the duty of the department to ascertain whether their statements are well-founded, and whether their grievances are as alleged. If, in view of the statement we had the other evening from the hon. Minister of the Interior, it can be established, as these moulders allege, that the government immigration agents in the old country are promoting and assisting this immigration under false pretenses, it is surely important enough to justify the interference of the hon. gentleman and his department. This movement is branching out and assuming more serious proportions, and the hon. gentleman should not hesitate to interfere and ascertain what the facts of the case are-who is in the right and who is in the wrong. In view of the policy enunciated by the hon. Minister of the Interior the other night, it is due to that hon. gentleman that the officials of his department should be absolved from the charges made against them by the Scotch moulders,
i
if they are not guilty of those charges. I have pointed out the serious effect that these statements will have on immigration. If these men are permitted to go back to Scotland and disseminate these statements as to the treatment they received from the government's agents in Scotland, and from those with whom they came in contact on shipboard or on this side of the Atlantic, l need not point out to the hon. gentleman that they will certainly have a depressing and serious effect, and I think he would be justified in inquiring and ascertaining all the facts and informing the people of Canada and the people of the old country as to the true condition of affairs.

This matter has acquired more than local importance ; and if the hon. Minister of Labour has not been asked by either side to interfere or conciliate, I think it would naturally be expected that the Labour Department would at all events keep track of the events that are happening in Toronto at the present time ; because we have evidently reached a crisis in dealing with labour matters in Ontario. I believe the minister will find it to be a matter that should be brought before the heads of other departments, notably, the Interior Department and the Justice - epartment. I have read the statements to which the hon. member for Toronto (Mr. Clarke) has called attention, and have taken the trouble to find out to what extent the complaints are well founded. There is one thing I am pleased to see, and that is that both sides in this case are laying the whole matter before the public. The men especially have taken great pains from the start to see that full information is given, and they took the very sensible step from the beginning of forbidding any of their own members picketting or besetting the premises included in the strike. There are several statements in the newspapers to-day, which I have ascertained to be true. One is that the county police have been instructed to arrest all men found around those premises. One result has been that two or three days ago three men, recently in the employ of the company, happened to be in that vicinity, and were taken in charge by the county police and rushed into the premises of the company. They were kept there several hours and then removed to one of the sub-police stations. On application being made for their release, the reply was given that they could not be released because no charge was made against them, and therefore it was not possible to bail them out. Later on a charge was made, and they were removed to the central police station. At 9.30 p.m, some friends of theirs wanted to bail them out, but they were told that it was contrary to custom to let men out after dark, so they were kept in jail all night. The next morning they were charged before the magistrate on an amended

charge, as the original charge was not properly made out, and they were then let out on bail. There is another matter to which I would call attention. The Noble Detective Agency has its men all around the works, following, watching, and besetting all men in any way connected with, or who have been in the employ of the company. These men are intimidated by the detectives and prevented doing things which they have a perfect right to do. As this is purely a labour trouble, the hon. minister should have these matters carefully watched and reported on to the Justice Department. The tact that a contract was made in the old country to bring these men out is a matter or public notoriety. That kind of thing has been oping ou during the last nine months very frequently, but during the last two years intermittently. During the earlier part of this session a large deputation of the Trade Congress of Canada, representing every province, waited on the government and urged it to pass an anti-contract law. But in this matter, as in every other, when the labouring people ask for an anti-contract labiur law, the impression is given foith that they are objecting to immigration of nil kinds. I wish distinctly to contradict that statement. In asking the government to pass an anti-contract labour law, they are asking it to do what lion, ministers have often admitted should be done. They have admitted that men snould not he en-cmi-aged by misrepresentations to come to Canada. Such contracts should be made illegal. The ordinary intelligent Canadian labouring man thoroughly appreciates the fact that when an Immigrant comes here and becomes a producer, he also becomes a consumer, but what we object to is bunging out workingmen under false represent^-tians ; to compete with the same class in our cities and towns. There is another department for which the hon. Minister of Labour could get some, information. In the interview with the First Minister of Ontario. I find this little passage :
As to protection, Mr. Barnett of the local union said they had met the employers In order to try and settle the dispute, and the employers asked the men to support them in I '^'-r agitation for a higher protective tariff, Mr. Barnett answered : * Why should we do so : You will not help us to protect labour, why should we help you to protect capital ?
I am told that there has been a movement going on during the last nine months to fl od our cities with artisans and mechanics, in order to have a glutted labour market and thus bring pressure on the government to raise the tariff. This is being done by the Manufacturers' Association which is fighting the battle of this foundry company and they are being sustained by the National Foundry Association, which is an international organization. What object have they in fighting us in this way ? Is their object

not also to congest the labour market, to make what they are pleased to call a fluid labour market, so that many will be without employment, and then they can turn around and say that what is wanted to give employment is more protection and a higher tariff. In this dispute which is now on in Toronto, there are a good many things concerning which the Labour Department should inform itself and in which it should not wait to oe asked to interfere. I am told that lorty citizens of Toronto, some of them with their families, have already crossed to the United States, and that in their places are these men who were brought from the old country, and who would be glad to return if they could get the price of their passage. To my mind, while an old country immigrant is a good immigrant, our Canadian people are the best people to keep in the country, and to have an organized movement driving our own men out and getting a more unstable population in, is injuring not only the province of Ontario, but the whole Dominion. This question is not a mere local one. It is a big contest with the International Association of Employers. This association sent over at the start from twenty to thirty men, contrary to the provisions of the Alien Labour Law. Why is that law not enforced ? This national association of employers keeps a hand of men, professional strike breakers, and brings them from Duluth and New York, and erects tents for them inside the foundry grounds and keeps them at work. Citizens of Toronto, who have gone on strike, cannot proceed against those men because they do not know their names, and we have the law violated by a large body of men who are supposed to be our best citizens. That matter should be looked into, and closely followed up. I claim that we have a right, while the Alien Labour Law is on the statute-book, to have it enforced. For myself, I am prepared at any time, if the hou. minister will oppose the repeal of that law, to vote with him, and to propose to the minister the introduction of an anti-contract labour law, to prevent workmen being brought here under contract to labour. There is no need for the introduction of such labour, and it is not brought here for any proper purpose. In the strike in Toronto all these features are found. As was stated in the paper to-day. when these old countrymen were brought in the cars in which they were were run within the company's works, and when they wanted to get out on Monday morning, they had to fight their way out. The police were there and the men had to fight their way out. And their baggage was stolen. Everything that has happened around these works for the last few days is having the effect of exciting and inciting men to riot. Tins is the natural effect of what is being done by the people who have lock-d-out their men; in fact, all the officials of the

719S
company, even aided by the police. That is the proper interpretation of their act when they deliberately force men to light their way out of the works-it is inciting to riot. There is no doubt that, if they are given time they will succeed. A large body of men cannot be expected, however peaceably disposed they may be, to remain impassive under irritation of this kind. It is important that the minister should keep close watch on the proceedings in Toronto until this matter is settled and get full and authentic information as to the various steps of what has occurred so far.
Miscellaneous-Department of Labour, allowances to correspondents, printing and stationery (including printing of ' Dabour Gazette), travelling expenses, &c., and $500 each for an accountant and French translator, which sum may be paid to any one in the civil service notwithstanding anything in the Civil Service Act, $33,450.
According to the Auditor General's Report the department spent only $32,213 for the year ending June 30th, 1902. How is it they need so much this year ?

It has bc-en usual to take an appropriation of $50,000 a year, but in no instance has this been required. Whatever is not used lapses. Ir. the fiscal year just closed there is a considerable lapse, and I trust there will be the same on the present vote. But the expenses of the department naturally increase. For instance, we have the ' Labour Gazette,' the printing of which is to be paid for out of this appropriation. The circulation has increased. At present I think it is between 11,000 and 12,000. It was established in August, 1900, so it will soon have completed its third year. There is a slight revenue from it, but not much-. Then, the committee *will remember that parliament this session has passed an Act under which the department may in tow me in railway labour disputes. That is another responsibility and duty placed i j:on the department. Whether it will involve any expense or not no one can tell. I trust that the railways of Canada will be free from labour disputes, but should they arise the expense will be provided for.
But why does the department require such a large vote when the Auditor General's Report shows a relatively small expenditure ?
That only show's that it is quite safe to trust us with the larger sum. We return directly ail	is not wanted.
What is the subscription price of the ' Labour Gazette ' and how many are subscribed for ?

The Labour Gazette can be obtained by annual
subscription or by separate copies. The annual subscription is 20c. and the price per copy 3e. There is a subscription list of between seven and eight thousand, besides a considerable free list. All members of parliament receive free copies, and public libraries throughout the country, boards of trade, &c., are also on the list.
What is the revenue ?
It would be 20 cents each on a subscription of between seven thousand and eight thousand ?
Last year it was $1,000.
That would show a subscription list, then, of about 5,000 copies.
What is the cost of producing it ?
It costs more than that. The amount is given in the Auditor General's Report.
I was not asking the Auditor General, but the Postmaster General.
r can get it and look it up.
Are there no advertisements in connection with the ' Labour Gazette ' ?
No.

As the items of the Labour Department will soon be passed, 1 would ask for an answer to a question I put with regard to the salaries of the British Columbia Labour Commissioners. I wished to know the date of beginning and the date of closing and the amount paid to each commissioner.

The commission was composed of Chief Justice Hunter and the Rev. Mr. Rowe. Chief Justice Hunter was paid $40 a day and Mr. Rowe was paid $35 a day. The secretary of the department was the Deputy Minister of Labour, who was not paid anything except his travelling expenses and the sum of $5 a day by way of indemnity to cover miscellaneous disbursements. The stenographer was Mr. Giddins, who was treated in the same manner, and allowed $5 a day for items of expenditure. The officers of the department left here on the 22nd of April and reached British Columbia in due course, going without a break to Victoria, where they put themselves in communication with the commissioners who immediately organized and published advertisements in the local press announcing the intention of the commission to begin the sittings. * Having given a few days' notice they commenced sittings in the first week of May and continued at their work, engaged either in taking evidence or in pre-

paring the report, without the break of a single day. They worked continuously from the time they began until the second week of July. Then the officers returned to the department, reaching here on the 18th of July. The cost of the commission, has not yet been ascertained. The hon. gentleman can figure it out to a certain, extent so far as these items go. But there is another large item to be paid for yet, that is the cost of publishing the report, and perhaps the evidence. The report is a voluminous one, covering about 170 pages of foolscap typewritten. There is also a vast amount of evidence, I am told over 3,000 pages. So if the evidence is also printed, it will involve a good deal of expenditure. I do not know whether the hon. gentleman thinks it would be advisable to publish the evidence. But as to the report, it is the intention to issue it as a supplement to the ' Gazette,' and for that purpose some 11,000 or 12,000 copies will be required. Other copies will als i be required,- and an order has been given for 15,000. I think it will be very instructive in regard to some of the causes of the labour troubles that have prevailed for som? time past.
Why not give us some of the causes now ?

The report is in the hands of the printers, I have not seen it yet. It reached here on the 18th of July. I felt that the best course to adopt would be to have it printed at once, and as soon as it is printed I will lay a copy upon the Table of the House. I have not yet been able myself to read through the report, although the deputy has stated to me a good deal of the substance of it.
Are we to understand that from the 22nd of April to the 18th of July inclusive, the commissioners received at the rate of $40 and $35 per day ?
They will only be paid from the time they began their work.
That is from the first week of May to the last of June.

From the day they began their work until they concluded it. I am sure that Chief Justice Hunter and the other commissioner could not think of charging any more than they are entitled to, and the Order in Council states specifically the amounts they are entitled to receive.
